tool.name: FractalDimension
tool.summary: Computes the local fractal dimension (surface roughness) of a DEM: for each cell, the fractal dimension D of the terrain within a moving window, from 2 (a smooth surface) to 3 (space-filling, maximally rough). Like the Vector Ruggedness Measure, it is independent of overall slope; it measures how roughness varies across scales. Four methods are offered -- triangular prism, variogram, madogram, and differential box counting -- which all estimate the same D but can give somewhat different values on real terrain.
tool.usage:
The fractal dimension D of a surface is a single number describing how rough or complex it is across scales: D = 2 for a perfectly smooth surface (a flat plane, or even a smoothly tilted plane) and rises toward D = 3 as the surface becomes so rough that it begins to fill three-dimensional space. Unlike the single-scale ruggedness tools (TRI, surface ratio, standard deviation), and like the Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM), fractal dimension is independent of the overall slope -- a smooth steep hillside scores D = 2, the same as flat ground -- because it measures how the amount of roughness changes as you look more or less closely, not the roughness at one fixed neighborhood size. That makes it a distinct kind of ruggedness: two surfaces can have the same slope and the same local relief yet different D (one smoothly rolling, the other crinkly at every scale).
A crucial point about fractal dimension is that it can be estimated in several different ways, and the different algorithms do not give exactly the same answer on real terrain. As Ju and Lam (2009) put it, "the problem of inconsistent results derived from different fractal calculation algorithms remains." This is not a defect of any one method: real terrain is only approximately fractal (fractal over a limited range of scales, and often different in different directions), so each algorithm -- which fits scaling in a different geometric or statistical domain -- returns a somewhat different value. All the methods here estimate the same quantity D, and all rise and fall together as a surface gets rougher, but they return different numbers even on artificial surfaces of known dimension, and they differ further on real DEMs. Choose one method and stay with it, and do not compare D values produced by different methods.
This tool offers four methods (see the Method parameter for the citation and a link for each):
The triangular prism method (Clarke 1986; local moving-window / divisor-step sampling by Ju and Lam 2009) measures how the three-dimensional surface area of the terrain shrinks toward its flat (planimetric) area as the measuring square grows, and derives D from the slope of that scaling. It is the classic method built specifically for topographic surfaces and is the closest relative of this toolbox's Surface Area and Ratio tool.
The variogram and madogram methods (Gneiting, Sevcikova, and Percival 2012, implemented in their R package fractaldim) come from spatial statistics: they measure how the elevation differences between cells grow with the distance between them, and derive D from that scaling. That distance is called the lag: at a lag of 1 every cell in the window is compared with its immediate neighbor along the row and along the column, at a lag of 2 with the cell two over, and so on. Each lag gives one typical elevation difference, and D comes from the slope of a straight line fitted through those values on logarithmic axes. By default the tool fits lags of 1 cell up to one third of the window (1 through 8 for a 25-cell window); Gneiting et al. fit only lags 1 and 2. On real DEMs the choice matters, because real terrain usually reads smoother at the shortest lags than at longer ones, so set Maximum lag if you want a specific range (2 reproduces their recipe). The lags used are reported in the run messages and recorded in the output's metadata. The madogram (mean absolute difference) is the estimator Gneiting et al. recommend, considering both efficiency and robustness; in their simulations the variogram had the lowest error on well-behaved data and the madogram was next. These two methods are amplitude-invariant -- their D does not depend on the vertical exaggeration at all -- so they are the most reliable default, and they reveal roughness on gentle as well as steep terrain.
Differential box counting (Sarkar and Chaudhuri 1994, with the box-counting rule of Li, Du, and Sun 2009) counts how many small three-dimensional boxes are needed to cover the surface at a series of box sizes, and derives D from that count. It is the box-counting representative, provided mainly for comparison with the wider fractal-dimension literature. It is the weakest of the three approaches in a moving window (see the note below).
Vertical and horizontal units: the triangular prism and box-counting methods use true one-to-one ground units -- elevation is measured against horizontal distance with no vertical exaggeration and no per-window normalization. If the DEM's elevation units differ from its horizontal (coordinate system) units -- for example elevation in feet on a meters projection -- set the Elevation units parameter and the tool converts internally so both are the same unit. A consequence of true one-to-one units is that these two methods reflect the terrain's actual three-dimensional shape: gently rolling terrain, whose relief is small relative to its cell size, is genuinely close to a plane and so reads near D = 2; only steep, broken terrain drives them toward 3. The variogram and madogram, being amplitude-invariant, reveal roughness regardless of steepness, which is another reason to prefer them as the default.
A note on window edges and sharp terrain boundaries (all methods): because the fractal dimension is estimated within a moving window, results near an abrupt boundary between two very different terrain types -- the flat rim and steep wall of a canyon, a cliff, or an escarpment -- can show a spurious ring or halo of high (or low) values within about half a window of the boundary. There the window straddles the boundary and analyzes a mixed surface that no single fractal dimension truly fits, so the estimate is unreliable. The width of this ring is set by the window, not by the terrain, so a telltale sign is that a band of extreme values sits about half a window from a sharp edge and moves outward if you increase the window size -- if it tracks the window, it is a window effect, not a real property of the ground. (Note also that a clean, steep wall on its own tends to read low, near 2, because a single dominant step is locally smooth in the fractal sense; the high values appear in the halo beside it, not on it.) The same caution applies within half a window of the raster edge or of any NoData gap. Smaller windows shrink the ring but give a noisier, less stable estimate -- a genuine trade-off.
A note on differential box counting: it is the weakest and noisiest of the three methods here, and its raw estimate can even fall slightly below the theoretical minimum of 2. Box counting fits a straight line to the count of boxes versus box size, but in a moving window only a handful of box sizes fit (for a 25-cell window, sizes 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12), and the box counts are coarse whole numbers, so the fitted slope is statistically noisy -- box counting is the least efficient of the estimators (Gneiting, Sevcikova, and Percival 2012). This gives it a compressed range (it separates smooth from rough terrain less sharply than the other methods) and its noisy slope can occasionally imply a value just under 2. Because a surface cannot truly have a fractal dimension below 2, all output is clipped to the range 2 to 3. It can also show a blocky, repeating pattern: the largest box sizes divide the window into only two or three whole tiles (for a 51-cell window the largest boxes, 24 and 16 cells, make two and three tiles), and those few coarse, grid-aligned, whole-number box counts stamp a repeating texture into the result at the scale of the boxes -- roughly a half and a third of the window. The triangular prism and variogram/madogram methods do not do this. Prefer the triangular prism or, especially, the variogram or madogram method when you need the most reliable local estimate.
The window is a square of the size you choose (odd, so it centers on each cell); larger windows give a more stable estimate but a coarser, more smoothed result and a wider NoData border. A window must be entirely free of NoData to produce a value, so cells within half a window of the raster edge or of any NoData gap are NoData in the output. The output is floating point, clipped to 2 to 3, and carries statistics and a histogram; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling. This tool reads the whole DEM into memory at once.
References: Clarke, K. C. 1986. Computation of the fractal dimension of topographic surfaces using the triangular prism surface area method. Computers and Geosciences 12(5):713-722. Ju, W., and N. S.-N. Lam. 2009. An improved algorithm for computing local fractal dimension using the triangular prism method. Computers and Geosciences 35(6):1224-1233 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cageo.2008.09.008). Gneiting, T., H. Sevcikova, and D. B. Percival. 2012. Estimators of fractal dimension: assessing the roughness of time series and spatial data. Statistical Science 27(2):247-277 (https://doi.org/10.1214/11-STS370); R package fractaldim (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=fractaldim). Sarkar, N., and B. B. Chaudhuri. 1994. An efficient differential box-counting approach to compute fractal dimension of image. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 24(1):115-120 (https://doi.org/10.1109/21.259692); box-counting rule (range divided by box height, rounded up, counted from each tile's own minimum): Li, J., Q. Du, and C. Sun. 2009. An improved box-counting method for image fractal dimension estimation. Pattern Recognition 42(11):2460-2469 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2009.03.001). The box itself is a true cube in ground units; the tool does not use their reduced box height or overlapping tiles.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the fractal dimension from. It must be single band. Both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are supported; on a geographic DEM a representative ground cell size at the DEM's centre latitude is used.

The output raster (floating point), the local fractal dimension D of each cell's neighborhood, clipped to the range 2 (smooth) to 3 (maximally rough). NoData wherever the moving window is not entirely within valid data. A suggested name is filled in from the input.

Which estimator to use. All four estimate the same fractal dimension D but by different models; they agree on ideal fractal surfaces and differ on real terrain, so pick one and stay with it (do not compare D across methods). The variogram or madogram is recommended as the most reliable default.

Triangular prism (Clarke 1986; Ju and Lam 2009): derives D from how the three-dimensional surface area shrinks toward the flat area as the measuring square grows. The classic topographic method. Uses true one-to-one ground units, so gentle terrain reads near 2. Clarke, K. C. 1986. Computers and Geosciences 12(5):713-722; Ju, W., and N. S.-N. Lam. 2009. Computers and Geosciences 35(6):1224-1233, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cageo.2008.09.008

Variogram (Gneiting, Sevcikova and Percival 2012): derives D from how squared elevation differences grow with distance between cells (the semivariance). Amplitude-invariant - independent of vertical exaggeration. Gneiting, T., et al. 2012. Statistical Science 27(2):247-277, https://doi.org/10.1214/11-STS370; R package fractaldim, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=fractaldim

Madogram (Gneiting, Sevcikova and Percival 2012): like the variogram but using the mean absolute difference rather than the squared difference; Gneiting et al. recommend it, considering both efficiency and robustness (in their simulations the variogram had the lowest error on well-behaved data, with the madogram next). Also amplitude-invariant. Same references as the variogram.

Differential box counting (Sarkar and Chaudhuri 1994): derives D from how many small boxes are needed to cover the surface at a series of box sizes. The box-counting representative, provided mainly for comparison with the wider literature; it is the weakest and noisiest of the methods in a moving window and its values are clipped up to 2 (see the tool help). Sarkar, N., and B. B. Chaudhuri. 1994. IEEE Trans. SMC 24(1):115-120, https://doi.org/10.1109/21.259692; box-counting rule: Li, Du and Sun 2009 (Pattern Recognition 42:2460-2469), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2009.03.001

The side length of the square moving window, in cells; must be odd and at least 9 (the default is 25). Larger windows give a more stable but coarser, more smoothed estimate and a wider NoData border near edges and gaps.

You enter a single window size - you do not enter step sizes or divisors; the tool derives those itself. The triangular prism method measures the surface at several step sizes that must divide the window evenly, so for that method pick a window size where (the window size minus 1) has several whole-number factors. Good choices are 13, 17, 25 (the default), 33, 37, 49, and 61, which each give four or more step sizes. Any odd size of 9 or more will run, but some give only three steps (23, for example, gives 1, 2, and 11) and a less stable fit. This constraint applies only to the triangular prism method - the variogram, madogram, and box-counting methods accept any odd window size.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say. Elevation is converted internally so that vertical and horizontal are the same ground unit (true one-to-one), which affects the triangular prism and box-counting methods; the variogram and madogram are amplitude-invariant and unaffected by this setting.

param.name: max_lag
param.displayname: Maximum lag (cells; variogram and madogram only)

dialogReference.para: The longest lag, in cells, used by the variogram and madogram methods. A lag is the distance between the two cells being compared: the tool compares every cell in the window with the cell 1 over, 2 over, and so on up to this value, along rows and columns, and fits D to how the typical elevation difference grows with that distance.

Leave it blank to use lags of 1 through one third of the window (1 through 8 for the default 25-cell window). Enter 2 to use only lags 1 and 2, the choice of Gneiting, Sevcikova, and Percival (2012), which measures roughness at the scale of one or two cells. Larger values bring in roughness at longer distances. The value must be between 2 and half the window size. Because the blank default grows with the window, enter a fixed value when you want to compare window sizes over the same range of distances.
This parameter is unavailable for the triangular prism and box-counting methods, which derive their own step and box sizes from the window size.

scriptExample.title: Fractal Dimension example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The recommended madogram estimator, then the triangular prism method for comparison.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.FractalDimension( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_FD_madogram", method="Madogram (Gneiting, Sevcikova & Percival 2012)", window_size=25, elev_units="Meters", max_lag=None) # None = lags 1 through one third of the window; 2 = Gneiting et al. arcpy.jenness.FractalDimension( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_FD_prism", method="Triangular prism (Clarke 1986; Ju & Lam 2009)", window_size=25, elev_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Local fractal dimension (surface roughness, D from 2 to 3) of a DEM in a moving window, by a selectable method (triangular prism, variogram, madogram, or differential box counting); like VRM, independent of overall slope.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the per-cell local fractal dimension of the terrain surface within a moving square window, a measure of roughness (D = 2 smooth, up to 3 maximally rough) that, like the Vector Ruggedness Measure, is independent of overall slope and instead captures how roughness varies across scales. Four estimators are offered, all of the same quantity D: the triangular prism method (Clarke 1986; local divisor-step version, Ju and Lam 2009), the variogram and madogram variation estimators (Gneiting, Sevcikova and Percival 2012, their R package fractaldim), and differential box counting (Sarkar and Chaudhuri 1994, with the box-counting rule of Li et al. 2009). Different algorithms give somewhat different values on real terrain (Ju and Lam 2009). The prism and box-counting methods use true one-to-one ground units (gentle terrain reads near 2); the variogram and madogram are amplitude-invariant and are the recommended default. Box counting is the weakest local estimator and its output is clipped up to 2. All output is clipped to [2, 3]; a window must be free of NoData to produce a value. The output carries statistics and a histogram.
